source.title: Mapping the Emergence of Regularization-Driven Dynamics in Grokking

record.tranche_reason: Tests grokking dynamics using transient regularization pulses and response/loss-barrier measurements, rather than reproducing the original studies’ methods.
record.gate_note: The paper also cites grokking and mechanistic-progress results from other work; those cited results are not recorded as rows. Its own checkpoint progress-measure analyses and transient regularization interventions are recorded.
record.test_reason: The study's own baseline runs show delayed generalization on three algorithmic tasks (V1). It applies the Nanda- and Barak-style progress measures to Task 1 (V2). Its transient weight-decay and ℓ1 pulses show that more regularization advances and less delays generalization (V5). Its method (sliding regularization pulses, mode-connectivity barriers) differs from the originals' but asks the same questions. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress that the dose-ordered regime emerges while test accuracy is still at chance, well before visible generalization. They report that in Task 1 standard static progress measures show little advance signal, whereas perturbation responses do. They interpret the pattern as consistent with regularization-driven motion along a stable slow manifold, calling it 'canalization of grokking solution selection', and limit the claim to small algorithmic tasks.
record.recipe_differences: Uses fixed-duration transient weight-decay or ℓ1 pulses across the pre-generalization plateau, rather than reproducing the original grokking or mechanistic-interpretability analyses. It measures timing shifts, loss barriers, and selected progress metrics.
record.method_sensitivity: Response ordering changes with pulse timing: early responses are unordered and later responses become dose-ordered. The onset and loss-barrier pattern differ across tasks; in Task 3 barriers are low before dose ordering emerges. Task 1 progress measures provide little advance signal.

fits_no_version.finding: As pulses move later, test-loss barriers between perturbed and baseline generalization checkpoints collapse toward zero while timing effects persist. In Task 3 barriers are low before ordering emerges; under ℓ1 the test barrier stays near zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Late in the grokking plateau, regularization perturbations change generalization timing but no longer redirect training to a linearly separated solution ('canalization').

fits_no_version.finding: In Task 1 the perturbation-response dose ordering appears ~4,000 epochs before the baseline crosses 0.90 test accuracy. Static progress measures give little signal over the same period (Appendix F).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Responses to transient perturbations can anticipate grokking earlier than static checkpoint progress measures.

fits_no_version.finding: PCA of update directions in Task 1: early pulses deviate from the baseline, while pulses at ordering onset follow overlapping paths (Appendix E, Fig. 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Same canalization claim as above; update-direction evidence.

record.code_released: Code, numerical results, and figure source data are stated to be provided in the supplementary material; URL not stated.
record.problems: Task 1 and Task 2 use screened grokking runs; Task 1’s principal dose-linearity summary uses 30 runs, Task 2 24, and Task 3 16. Several outcomes are qualitative in the text or shown in figures rather than numerically tabulated. The authors state that the work is limited to small algorithmic tasks and that generalization-time definitions may be harder in more complex tasks.

untested.parts: Dependence of the delay on training-set size; only one training-set size per task.
The Fourier algorithm for modular addition (progress measures applied only to Task 1 parity match); direct evidence that memorizing components are removed.
Circuit efficiency comparison, critical dataset size, and ungrokking below it.
Not tested: no non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or weight-norm regime sweep.
Not tested: algorithms learned across runs are not identified or compared.
Not tested: always AdamW (Adam for ℓ1), with no optimizer or floating-point controls.

missing.what: Prevalence of grokking under the screening criteria: Task 1 177/1,000 reach ≥0.95 and 105/1,000 qualify; Task 2 24/508 qualify; Task 3 needed no screening.
Baseline global weight norm trajectories: Task 1 shows little sustained decline until test loss improves; Tasks 2–3 show clearer late-training norm contraction.
Branches that fail to reach 0.95 test accuracy by epoch 40,000 (gray cells) after some pulses, which could indicate grokking switched off; frequency is not quantified.

record.verdict_notes: The V2 challenge rests on the parity-match task only. The authors cite that progress measures do anticipate grokking in sparse parity and modular addition, but they do not test those tasks themselves. The V5 support concerns only the direction of regularization's effect on timing; nothing in the study tests efficiency, critical dataset size or ungrokking. Reader's V5 limits_scope label on norm and barrier rows was removed: those rows either don't measure a V5 quantity or concern untested parts.

versions.untested_parts: Tests delayed generalization on selected algorithmic-task runs, but does not test whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks.

Measures selected static progress measures in Task 1, including a joint-parity Fourier feature, but does not identify a modular-addition Fourier algorithm or directly test whether memorizing circuits are removed.
No non-algorithmic image, text, or molecule task, and no initialization-scale or weight-norm regime sweep.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.

Tests effects of transient changes to regularization on generalization timing and measures global norm, but does not test whether the selected circuit is more efficient, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below it.
Does not identify and compare algorithms learned across runs.
Does not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point/softmax artifacts, or control for them.
